result: Bioluminescence imaging using GFP-Aequorin in motor neurons distinguishes locomotor behaviors. GFP-Aequorin was selectively expressed in spinal motor neurons without muscle expression (C12). Acoustic stimulation triggered escape responses (C13) and occasionally slow swims (C14). Escape responses generated larger bioluminescence amplitudes than slow swims (30.8 vs 4.1 photons/10 ms, C15), and bioluminescence amplitude correlated with tail bend angle (R=0.4, C16), suggesting increased motor neuron recruitment during behaviors with larger tail bends and faster frequencies (C17, C69).
evaluation: Claims C12-C17 and C69 provide converging evidence from immunohistochemistry, behavioral tracking, and bioluminescence measurements with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.001). The correlation analysis (C16) and the differential amplitudes between behaviors (C15) support the interpretation that bioluminescence amplitude reflects motor neuron recruitment patterns. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10 larvae, 283 stimulations).

result: Motor neuron recruitment patterns differ between slow swimming and escape responses. During fictive locomotion at 4 dpf, slow swims (20-30 Hz) recruited 23.2% of ventral motor neurons (C18, C20), while escapes (20-80 Hz) recruited 88.4% of motor neurons including dorsal populations (C19, C21). Dorsalmost motor neurons showed larger calcium transients (C22), and mean ΔF/F was higher during escapes (91.1% vs 25.9%, C23). The high bioluminescence during escapes results from both increased cell recruitment and larger calcium transients per neuron (C24-C26).
evaluation: Claims C18-C26 are well-supported by calcium imaging data with appropriate controls (n=10 larvae for GCaMP6f experiments). The combination of ventral nerve root recordings and calcium imaging provides complementary evidence. Statistical significance is properly reported (p<0.001), and the interpretation linking bioluminescence to both cell number and calcium amplitude is logically sound given the data.

result: Mechanosensory feedback enhances motor neuron recruitment during active locomotion. Bioluminescence amplitude decreased markedly after paralysis (26.6 vs 11.1 photons/10 ms, C27) with seven-fold reduction in normalized amplitude (C28). Immotile cacnb1 mutants showed similarly reduced bioluminescence compared to motile siblings (9.8 vs 37.6 photons/10 ms, C29). These results demonstrate enhanced motor neuron recruitment during active locomotion (C30, C31, C70, C71), indicating mechanosensory feedback contributes to increasing spinal motor output.
evaluation: Claims C27-C31, C70-C71 are supported by two complementary experimental approaches (pharmacological paralysis and genetic mutants) with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.001). The use of cacnb1 mutants (C29) controls for potential confounds from cholinergic receptor blockade. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10 larvae for paralysis, n=3 for mutants). The interpretation that mechanosensory feedback enhances motor output is well-justified.

result: Silencing mechanosensory neurons via BoTxBLC expression reduces locomotor speed and frequency. The isl2b promoter drives expression in mechanosensory neurons including Rohon-Beard neurons and dorsal root ganglia (C32). BoTxBLC+ animals showed reduced tail-beat frequency (34.2 vs 37.8 Hz, C35) and speed (56.9 vs 64.1 mm/s, C36), with increased escape duration (182.0 vs 168.1 ms, C37). The first C-bend amplitude was unaffected (C38), but subsequent tail bend amplitudes increased, especially ipsilaterally (C39).
evaluation: Claims C32, C35-C39 are supported by high-throughput kinematic analysis with large sample sizes (n=304 larvae, 890 escapes) and appropriate statistical tests. The expression pattern is confirmed by immunohistochemistry (C32). The selective effects on post-C-bend parameters (C38-C39) suggest specific modulation of motor circuits after response onset. Statistical significance is properly reported for all comparisons.

result: Mechanosensory feedback selectively enhances the fast component of escape responses. Within the fast regime (>30 Hz), silencing mechanosensory feedback reduced distance (5.9 vs 7.4 mm, C40), duration (60.0 vs 67.8 ms, C41), oscillations (2.9 vs 3.6, C42), speed (104.3 vs 112.6 mm/s, C43), and TBF (45.8 vs 48.4 Hz, C44). The reduction in speed and frequency is specifically restricted to the fast component (C50).
evaluation: Claims C40-C44, C50 are supported by detailed kinematic analysis separating fast and slow components using a 30 Hz cutoff based on prior literature. All comparisons show statistical significance (p≤0.005) with large sample sizes (n=1013 fast components). The selective effect on the fast component is a key finding that distinguishes this from global motor deficits.

result: Mechanosensory feedback promotes transition from fast to slow locomotion. Within the slow component (≤30 Hz), silencing mechanosensory feedback increased distance (3.5 vs 2.4 mm, C45), duration (140.9 vs 97.1 ms, C46), and oscillations (2.8 vs 1.9, C47), but had no effect on speed (C48) or TBF (C49). Mechanosensory feedback enhances speed by promoting the transition between fast and slow locomotion during escapes (C51).
evaluation: Claims C45-C49, C51 are supported by kinematic analysis with appropriate statistics (p<0.001 for significant effects, p=0.5 for non-significant). The differential effects on fast vs slow components (increased slow duration but unchanged slow speed) support the interpretation that mechanosensory feedback controls the timing of the fast-to-slow transition (C51). Sample size is adequate (n=1265 slow components).

result: Rohon-Beard neurons form monosynaptic connections onto dorsal V2a interneurons. Anatomical observations showed perisomatic innervation of dorsal V2a neurons by RB axons (C54). RB neurons required 200-700 pA to spike (C55) while V2a neurons required only 15-50 pA (C56). Optogenetic stimulation with 1-5 ms light pulses elicited RB spikes (C57) and short-latency EPSCs in V2a neurons (3.71 ms delay, C58). The 0.9 ms lag between RB spike and V2a EPSC onset is compatible with monosynaptic connection (C59), with estimated conduction velocity of 0.75 m/s (C60). EPSC amplitude averaged 28.14 pA, producing ~11.71 mV depolarization (C61), sufficient to elicit V2a spikes in some cases (C62). Glutamatergic blockers abolished EPSCs (C63), confirming monosynaptic glutamatergic connection (C64) that selectively recruits fast V2a interneurons (C65).
evaluation: Claims C54-C65 provide converging evidence from anatomy, electrophysiology, optogenetics, and pharmacology. The timing analysis (C59) uses appropriate criteria from cited literature (3 ms cutoff). Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-8 cells). The conduction velocity calculation (C60) is consistent with prior measurements. The pharmacological validation (C63) confirms glutamatergic transmission. The integration of multiple experimental approaches strongly supports the monosynaptic connection.

result: Mechanosensory feedback enhances motor pool recruitment, increases locomotor speed by prolonging fast swimming, and involves monosynaptic RB-V2a connections. These are the primary findings stated in the abstract, integrating behavioral, imaging, and circuit mapping data.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript and are supported by the detailed experimental results grouped in other result clusters. C1 is supported by bioluminescence and calcium imaging data. C2 is supported by kinematic analysis of BoTxBLC animals. C3 is supported by optogenetic circuit mapping. All three claims are well-justified by the experimental evidence.

result: The RB-V2a pathway may act with other mechanosensory inputs to enhance speed (C66). Mechanosensory feedback allows larvae to travel the same distance ~15 ms faster (C67), potentially enhancing survival during predator attacks (C68).
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are speculative interpretations. C66 acknowledges that DRG and trigeminal neurons may also contribute, but this is not directly tested. C67 infers the 15 ms time savings from the duration data but doesn't directly measure it. C68 proposes ecological implications without survival experiments. These are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental validation.

result: Background on V2a interneurons and mechanosensory feedback from prior literature. V2a interneurons are recruited frequency-dependently (C4) in distinct microcircuit modules (C5), and their ablation affects coordination and gait (C6, C7). Mechanosensory feedback sets timing of muscle activation (C8), can reorganize motor output (C9), and perturbations affect motor sequences (C10, C11).
evaluation: Claims C4-C11 are properly cited background claims from prior literature. They provide context for the current study but are not new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims accurately represent the cited work based on the descriptions provided.

result: Additional background claims from prior literature on V2a interneurons, mechanosensory systems in fish and other species, and comparisons between active and fictive locomotion across species.
evaluation: Claims C52-C53, C72-C85, C87-C93 are properly cited background claims that provide context for the study. They accurately represent prior work based on the citations provided. These are not new findings but establish the scientific foundation for the current experiments.

result: RB neurons have complex processes (C86). Microcircuit selection results from combined descending and local spinal sensorimotor inputs (C94).
evaluation: C86 is established anatomical knowledge. C94 is a reasonable inference from the experimental findings showing that mechanosensory feedback modulates motor output during active locomotion, suggesting that circuit selection involves both descending commands and local sensory feedback. This interpretation is well-justified by the data.

result: Methodological details on transgenic line generation and characterization. The mnx1:gal4 line was generated using constructs from collaborators (C95), GFP-Aequorin was codon-optimized (C96), and cacnb1 mutants have impaired calcium release causing immobility (C97).
evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are methodological details that are appropriately documented. C95-C96 describe transgenic line generation with proper attribution. C97 accurately describes the cacnb1 mutant phenotype based on the cited original characterization. These are necessary technical details but not primary findings.
